title: Plain silk, uncarved wood
hookLine: show plainness, embrace simplicity, have few desires (Tao Te Ching 19)

cards: Two pieces of wood on a workbench. One is a finished carving: a bird, every feather cut in, polished, perfect. The other is a plain block, straight from the tree, nothing done to it yet.
Which one could still become anything? The bird is beautiful, and it will only ever be a bird. The block could be a bowl, a spoon, a bird, a handle, a toy.
Chapter nineteen of the Tao Te Ching reaches for that block. Its name for it is a single word, pu.

teach.h: GIVE UP CLEVERNESS AND THE NAMED VIRTUES.
teach.b: First, the chapter starts by throwing things out. Give up sageliness and cleverness, it says, and the people will be better off.
Give up kindness and righteousness, and the people will return to devotion and care in their families. Give up craftiness and profit, and there'll be no thieves.
It picks up where yesterday left off: the named virtues came after the way was lost, so let the names go. Second, it admits that's not enough.
Throwing things out leaves a hole, and people need something to hold on to. So it offers three things: show plainness, embrace the uncarved, be less selfish and want less. Third, the two pictures.
Plainness here is su, raw silk, undyed, the cloth before anyone colors it.
The uncarved is pu, wood in the block, before anyone shapes it. Both are materials in their first state: not poor, not ugly, just not yet worked over.

A person, like silk or wood, can be dyed and carved by praise, ambition, cleverness and wanting, until there's no room left to become anything else. Fourth, what it isn't. Pu isn't a call to be simple-minded.
Some readers hear an invitation to stay a little unfinished, to keep some of yourself raw and plain, with room to grow in a new direction.
The carving is admired. The block is free.

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take pu, the uncarved block, as a reason to keep their lives and belongings plain, and to leave room in themselves for what isn't finished yet.

games.q: chapter nineteen has just told people to give up cleverness, the named virtues and profit. what does it do next?
o: offer something to hold: plainness, the uncarved, few desires.
write a new set of rules.
games.why: it admits throwing things out isn't enough, so it gives three things to hold on to.

practice: Rest your eyes on one plain thing near you, a cotton shirt, a wooden spoon, a white mug, a glass of water, and notice it as it is, with nothing added: its weight, its color, its texture.
Then turn the same attention to yourself, the part of you before titles and opinions and plans: not better, not worse, just plain and uncarved.
